text: After two lessons of real, meaningful syntax differences — legacy Oracle joins, and two different keywords for the same correlated-subquery trick — this lesson is good news. Common table expressions, the WITH clause, are one of the more portable corners of modern SQL. You'll see why in a moment: almost everything about them is identical across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL. There's exactly one real wrinkle, and it only shows up with recursive CTEs.

Here's a plain CTE in T-SQL: WITH HighValueCustomers AS, a subquery that groups and filters, then a SELECT against the CTE by name. Now picture the identical query on Oracle, on MySQL 8-point-0 or later, or on PostgreSQL — the shape doesn't change at all. Same WITH keyword, same parenthesized subquery, same ability to reference the CTE by name afterward. If you can write a CTE in T-SQL, you can already write one correctly on any of these other three platforms, no translation needed.

One important version floor to know, though: MySQL only gained CTE support starting in MySQL 8-point-0. If you're working against MySQL 5.7 or earlier, WITH doesn't exist at all — you'd have to fall back to a derived subquery instead. Always confirm the MySQL version before assuming CTEs are available. Oracle and T-SQL have supported CTEs for a long time, and PostgreSQL has supported them since version 8.4, so this version concern is specifically a MySQL consideration.

Now the recursive case, which is where the one real divergence lives. Here's a recursive CTE in T-SQL, walking an employee hierarchy: an anchor member — the top-level employees with no manager — unioned all with a recursive member that joins Employees back to EmployeeHierarchy itself, adding one to the level each time. Oracle writes this exact same shape, no special keyword required. The engine recognizes the self-reference inside the recursive member and just handles it.

MySQL 8-point-0 and PostgreSQL need one extra word: WITH RECURSIVE, not just WITH. Everything else about the query — the anchor member, the UNION ALL, the recursive member referencing the CTE by name — is written exactly the same way. Leave out RECURSIVE on either of these two platforms, and the self-reference to employee_hierarchy inside the recursive member fails to parse; the engine won't allow a CTE to reference itself without that keyword present.

So here's the full picture to carry forward: plain CTEs are essentially universal, with MySQL's 8-point-0 version floor as the only catch. Recursive CTEs need the word RECURSIVE on MySQL and PostgreSQL, but not on T-SQL or Oracle — everything else about the anchor-member, recursive-member shape is identical across all four. Next lesson, we look at a case with one genuine naming difference worth memorizing: UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT, versus Oracle's own name for that last one, MINUS.
